sender: Nadia Ferreira, Head of Research, GridSense Analytics
subject: GridSense AI Load Index (Sept): metered IT load at 140 AI halls - non-hyperscaler utilization falls to 63%, Hopper-to-Blackwell migration slower than modeled
body:
Hi Larchmont Ridge team,

Our September AI Load Index is out. The headline finding runs against the prevailing "everything is sold out" narrative on AI compute for non-hyperscaler customers.

Method: We read sub-metered IT power draw at 140 AI-designated data halls (47 operators) across 9 U.S. and European markets and convert it to a load factor, meaning measured draw divided by contracted critical power. Halls are classified by the accelerator generation reported by the operator or our sensor mapping.

September results (load factor, vs. June):
- All AI halls: 63% (June: 74%)
- Hyperscaler-operated halls (n=38): 82% (-1pt)
- Neocloud and colo AI halls (n=71): 54% (June: 71%)
- Enterprise/sovereign halls (n=31): 49% (June: 58%)

By accelerator generation:
- Hopper halls: 41% (June: 66%)
- Blackwell/GB200 halls: 80% (June: 83%)

Why this matters: Hopper capacity at neoclouds is going idle faster than the market assumes. 22 of 71 neocloud halls show load below 40% for three consecutive weeks. Idle Hopper capacity reduces the incentive to buy Blackwell racks and strains the financing behind existing fleets. The Street's FQ3/FQ4 Nvidia models assume non-hyperscaler data center revenue grows about +9% q/q, in line with the commentary from management. Our data is consistent with flat to down, and we would flag the growth assumptions for neocloud and enterprise demand as most at risk. Hyperscaler loads remain full.

Caveats: Load factor is not a perfect proxy for utilization (reserved but idle capacity can still pay). 26 halls had sensor gaps, and November data will help confirm.

The full dataset (hall-level, anonymized) and a methodology note are attached. We can walk your team through the data on a call this week.
